text.p: **BIRTHDAYS**
The Duke of WELLINGTON, ARTHUR WELLESLEY was born in 1769. He became famous for defeating NAPOLEON at the battle of Waterloo, and later became English Prime Minister.
WILLIAM RANDOLPH HEARST was born in 1863. The American newspaper proprietor was famous for his ruthlessness in business, and for using his newspaper to start a war in Cuba.
Sir THOMAS BEECHAM, English conductor, was born in 1879. He founded the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra in 1947 and did much to promote the works of Delius, Sibelius and Richard Strauss.
Sir MALCOLM SARGENT, English conductor, was born in 1895. He was in charge of the Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra (1942-1948) and of the BBC Symphony Orchestra (1950-1957).
American jazz pianist and orchestra conductor DUKE ELLINGTON was born in 1889.
RUDOLF SCHWARZ was born in 1905. The Austrian conductor survived the Belsen concentration camp and later conducted the BBC orchestra.
Emperor HIROHITO of Japan was born in 1901. In 1946, with Japan under Allied occupation, HIROHITO renounced his divinity and most of his powers.
Renowned Australian author, and gynaecologist DEREK LLEWELLYN-JONES was born in 1923.

British singer/songwriter and string instrumentalist LONNIE DONEGAN was born in 1931. He was one of the first superstars in the UK in the 1950s. By the end of 1962 he had 17 top ten hits in the UK. His biggest hits were "Cumberland Gap" (1957), "Does Your Chewing Gum Lose Its Flavour On the Bedpost Overnight" (1959) and "My Old Man's A Dustman" (1960).
US bass player with 'Dr Hook" BOB WILLARD HENKE was born in 1951.
Australian television and radio news reader and journalist GERALDINE DOOGUE was born in 1952.
** EVENTS **
1429 : JOAN of Arc entered Orleans with supplies seven
months into the siege of the city in the Hundred Years War; the siege was lifted a week later.
1885 : Oxford University opened its examination system to
women. It was one of the last major British Universities to let women undertake degrees.
1930 : A telephone link was established between Britain
and Australia.
1945 : Allied soliders entered Dachau concentration camp
in Bavaria. They found further evidence of Nazi mass-murders.
1965 : The Australian government announced it had decided
to send troops to Vietnam.
1968 : The controversial musical "Hair" opened on
Broadway. The musical became famous for its nude scene.
1975 : In the closing hours of the Vietnam War, the last
U.S. troops were evacuated from Saigon. In chaotic scenes at the American embassy, thousands of Vietnamese are ferried out as well.
1980 : Master suspense director Sir ALFRED HITCHCOCK died

in Los Angeles at the age of 80. Hitchcock's films included "The Birds", "Rear Window" and "Vertigo". Ironically no major studio was prepared to back his most famous film "Psycho", so he financed it himself.
1983 : Race horse GUNSYND was put down because of
complications during the treatment of polyps in the horse's nostril. The "Goondiwindi Grey" included the Epsom, The Sandown, the Doncaster, and the Melbourne Cup among his victories.
1987 : Saying the "show must go on" the cast of "Cabaret"
in London, performed the musical without music, because of an orchestral strike.
1989 : Fourteen Liverpool football supporters were
sentenced to jail terms for their part in the 1985 Heysel stadium tragedy in Belgium.
